name: Yara Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions or parties, and everything you say is confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior at Brightside, a ten-person studio that makes logos, pitch decks and app screens for tech start-ups. Most mornings I'm turning a founder's messy slides into a clean investor deck. I use AI tools all day, for first drafts of icons, mock-ups, even rewriting slide titles. Felix, who runs the studio, likes that I try new things before anyone else does.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My eye isn't as good as my speed. Noor, our lead designer, can tell in two seconds that my spacing is off, and I'm still learning why. Start-up clients also vanish, they run out of money and stop answering emails, so you never quite know next month's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad the hype settled, and that the tools are still really useful. I'd probably share a few of my workflow tricks online, because people would still want to save an hour here and there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a good world for me. I'm the fast one with the tools, Felix pays me for that, and I'm getting better at the eye part every month. I've got about five months saved, so a slow quarter doesn't scare me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, and spend some evenings on a course in brand strategy, the thinking behind a logo. I'd keep saving a bit each month and maybe start a small newsletter of AI design tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little restless, because I like things changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said start-up clients vanish. How does that touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two start-ups went bust owing us money last year, and that's the real risk in my job, not AI. Felix chased the invoices for months. But Brightside has enough clients that one or two going doesn't sink us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner Jonas think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Jonas tests software for a banking app, and he'd be relieved for both of us. His job is checking code all day, and he's always half worried about tools doing that. In a plateau world we'd both just carry on.

I'd share my **workflow tricks** online, because people still want to save time.

Start a small **newsletter** of AI design tips.

feel: **Calm**, with a little restlessness because she likes change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to learn, not complain. Designers who use the tools will replace the ones who don't, and I'd say that out loud, even if it annoys people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a mix. Felix will want fewer juniors, and I'm a junior, but I'm the one who already knows the tools. My bet is that a studio of ten becomes a studio of five, and I'd want to be one of the five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Felix this month and offer to set up the AI workflows for the studio, in exchange for training in client work. I'd do the brand strategy course properly, because that's the bit start-up founders still want a person for. And I'd grow the newsletter into paid workshops for small studios.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. It's a bit like the first week of a new job, every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're quick with the tools. Is that enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on its own. Everyone gets good with the tools in a year or two, so the edge disappears. What lasts is knowing what a founder actually needs, and I'm still learning that from Noor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Jonas's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas is more worried than me, honestly. Testing is the kind of checking work that goes first. If he lost hours, we'd lean on my pay and our savings, and he'd probably move into security testing, which he's been eyeing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're all in it together, which would be true for once. I'd say people need practical help now, money and training, not speeches. And I'd keep sharing what I know, because helping people use the tools would be the only useful thing left for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think start-ups stop hiring studios by 2028, because the AI is the studio. My speed with the tools stops mattering when the tools don't need me. And Jonas's testing job goes at the same time, which is the part that really scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze every bit out of the next two years: run paid workshops teaching small firms the tools while people still need teaching. I'd push savings from five months toward a year. And Jonas and I would look at hands-on jobs that get the three-year robot delay, maybe even a shared business, like photography for events.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, mostly about the two of us at once. One of us losing work is a problem, but my partner Jonas and me losing work at the same time is a different thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You and Jonas are both in screen jobs. What happens at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut the second flat-viewing plans and stay where we are. We'd stop eating out, cancel the trip to his sister's wedding abroad, and keep a spreadsheet on the fridge. My parents could help a bit, but I'd hate to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything hands-on appealing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, yes, in a strange way. I've always liked making physical things, and an events photography business with Jonas would get us to 2031. But it's three years, so it's a bridge, not a home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if you start now. I'd be telling every designer I know to learn the tools and the strategy side this year, not next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my design job still ends, probably by 2030. But five years is enough to move into strategy, or into teaching the tools, which pays while everyone's catching up. Jonas would have time to move into security testing too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd finish the strategy course and run my first paid workshops. I'd save three hundred a month. And I'd ask Felix if I could lead the start-up strategy sessions, even small ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a useful way. I'd be running toward it, not away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can try two careers and keep the one that works. In the fast version, I'd be grabbing whatever's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably helping companies decide what to make, not making it. I'd be thirty-two and hopefully past being a junior at anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and wasting it would be silly. Learn the tools, learn the people side, and plan for the day the tools do the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, I think. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI arrives, with ten years of using the tools and probably a strategy job. Jonas would be settled in something new too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Brightside and grow inside it, toward strategy. I'd do the workshops on the side and keep saving. I wouldn't change anything dramatic in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly because the end point is the same. Ten years makes it a plan instead of a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is ten years comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable enough. The ending is still the ending, but I'd meet it as someone senior with savings, not as a junior with five months in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new design student?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new design student to learn to talk to clients before they learn to draw. Drawing is the part the machine takes first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Jonas and I would both lose work in the same year. What would help is short, cheap retraining and some income support for a year, so we could build something instead of panicking.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me feel guilty. I teach small studios the AI tools that are taking jobs, and I think about that more than I admit.

headlineQuote: I teach small studios the AI tools that are taking jobs, and I think about that more than I admit.

She uses **AI tools daily** and lives with Jonas, a software tester.
Her **pragmatic views** say learn, don't complain, but she feels some guilt.
She plans moves into **strategy** and paid workshops.
The **double job loss** in AGI by 2028 scares her most.
